::: {.at-a-glance}
- **Time:** 30 to 60 minutes, at home, before the first hands-on lesson ([lesson 02](02-project-organization.qmd)).
- **You need:** a laptop (macOS, Linux or Windows 10/11) with 10 GB free disk space, and an internet connection.
- **You will have:** Pixi, Git and a GitHub account, and a cache of the software we use in class.
:::

## Overview

In this course almost all software comes from one tool, **Pixi**. You install
Pixi once; Pixi then installs Python, Quarto, Jupyter, the bioinformatics
tools, Snakemake and Nextflow *inside each project*, at the exact versions the
project asks for. That is the main idea of the course in one sentence: the
project, not your laptop, decides which software it runs with.

**Learning outcome.** After this page you can install Pixi on your own
computer and use it to run a program you never installed (`pixi exec`). The
setup check at the end proves it.

### Choose your setup

| Your computer | What you do |
|---------------|-------------|
| macOS (Apple silicon or Intel) | Work in the **Terminal** app. Follow the *macOS / Linux* tabs. |
| Linux | Work in your terminal. Follow the *macOS / Linux* tabs. |
| Windows 10 or 11 | Install **WSL2** with Ubuntu (step 1), then work in the Ubuntu terminal and follow the *macOS / Linux* tabs. |
| Nothing works, or a locked-down computer | Use **GitHub Codespaces** in the browser (step 7). |

Why WSL2 on Windows? Several tools we use (`bwa`, `samtools`, `bcftools`)
are not built for Windows at all. We checked on 2026-10-24: conda-forge and
bioconda have Linux and macOS builds of these tools, but no Windows (`win-64`)
builds. Inside WSL2 your laptop runs a real Linux, so everything works.

## 1. Windows only: install WSL2

Open **PowerShell as Administrator** (right-click, "Run as administrator") and run:

```powershell
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
```

Restart when asked. Ubuntu then opens and asks you to choose a Linux user name
and password (they do not need to match your Windows ones). From now on,
**open "Ubuntu" from the Start menu** whenever this course says "terminal",
and follow the *macOS / Linux* instructions.

::: {.callout-tip}
Keep your course files inside Linux (for example `~/cbio7501`), not under
`/mnt/c/...`: it is much faster. To see your Linux files in Windows Explorer,
run `explorer.exe .` in the Ubuntu terminal.
:::

Microsoft's guide: <https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install>.

## 2. Open a terminal

- **macOS:** Applications → Utilities → Terminal.
- **Linux:** your terminal application.
- **Windows:** the Ubuntu (WSL2) app from step 1.

Check which shell you have; the answer is usually `bash` or `zsh`:

```{.bash .run}
echo "$SHELL"
```

New to the terminal? [Bash 101](C-bash.qmd) is an hour of practice with the
commands the lessons use. Do it before lesson 02.

## 3. Install Pixi

::: {.panel-tabset group="os"}

### macOS / Linux (and WSL2)

```{.bash .norun}
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh
```

The installer puts `pixi` in `~/.pixi/bin` and adds that folder to your
`PATH` in `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`. **Close the terminal and open a new
one** so the change takes effect.

### Windows (native PowerShell, optional)

You do not need this if you work in WSL2. For completeness:

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm -useb https://pixi.sh/install.ps1 | iex"
```

:::

Check that it works:

```{.bash .run}
pixi --version
```

Expected output (your version can be newer):

```text
pixi 0.83.0
```

::: {.callout-note title="Telemetry: what the installer sends"}
The install script sends one anonymous "installation ping" to prefix.dev, the
company behind Pixi. To opt out, set `PIXI_NO_TELEMETRY=1` before installing:
`curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | PIXI_NO_TELEMETRY=1 sh`.
Details: <https://pixi.sh/latest/reference/telemetry/>.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Already have Pixi?"}
Update it with `pixi self-update`. Anything from version 0.60 on works with
this course; we test with 0.83.0.
:::

### Optional: tab completion

Tab completion saves typing. Add one line to your shell's start-up file, then
open a new terminal:

::: {.panel-tabset group="shell"}

### bash

```{.bash .norun}
echo 'eval "$(pixi completion --shell bash)"' >> ~/.bashrc
```

### zsh (macOS default)

```{.bash .norun}
echo 'autoload -Uz compinit && compinit' >> ~/.zshrc
echo 'eval "$(pixi completion --shell zsh)"' >> ~/.zshrc
```

:::

## 4. Run software you never installed

This is the first taste of Pixi. `pixi exec` downloads a program into a
temporary environment and runs it. Nothing is installed on your system:

```{.bash .run}
pixi exec python --version
pixi exec --spec "quarto>=1.9" quarto --version
```

The first run takes a minute (it downloads packages); the second run of the
same command is fast because Pixi keeps a cache.

## 5. Git and GitHub

### Install Git

Check whether you already have Git (version 2.28 or newer):

```{.bash .run}
git --version
```

If the command is not found, install Git with Pixi. `pixi global` installs a
tool for your user, outside any project:

```{.bash .norun}
pixi global install git
```

::: {.callout-note}
On macOS, `git --version` may offer to install Apple's "command line developer
tools". Accept, or use `pixi global install git` instead.
:::

### Tell Git who you are

Use the same email address as on GitHub. Replace the example values:

```{.bash .run-ci}
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.org"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor nano
```

The third line makes new repositories start on a branch called `main`, as on
GitHub. The last one makes Git open nano, an easy editor, when it needs a
message from you; otherwise it often opens vim, which is hard to leave the
first time ([Terminal editors and sessions](D-terminal.qmd)).

The email is written into every commit, and anyone can read it once you push
to a public repository. To keep your address private, use the *noreply*
address that GitHub shows under **Settings → Emails** (it looks like
`12345678+ada-lovelace@users.noreply.github.com`).

### Create a GitHub account and an SSH key

1. Create a free account at <https://github.com/signup> if you do not have one.
   As a student you can also ask for the free
   [GitHub Education](https://education.github.com/) benefits.
2. GitHub needs a key, not a password, when you upload from the terminal.
   Follow GitHub's two short guides:
   [generate an SSH key](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/generating-a-new-ssh-key-and-adding-it-to-the-ssh-agent)
   and [add it to your account](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/adding-a-new-ssh-key-to-your-github-account).
3. Test the connection. The answer should greet you by your user name:

```{.bash .norun}
ssh -T git@github.com
```

## 6. Docker (needed for lesson 08) {#docker}

Install Docker before [lesson 08](08-containers.qmd):

- macOS and Windows: [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/get-docker/).
  On Windows, turn on "Use the WSL 2 based engine" so Docker works inside Ubuntu.
- Linux: [Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) and the
  [post-install steps](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/linux-postinstall/)
  so you can run Docker without `sudo`.

Check it:

```{.bash .norun}
docker run --rm hello-world
```

A free [Docker Hub](https://hub.docker.com/) account is optional; in lesson
08 we push images to the GitHub Container Registry with your GitHub account.

## 7. The fallback: GitHub Codespaces

If installing fails, or your computer does not let you install software, use
a Codespace: a Linux computer in the browser with Pixi already installed.

1. Open <https://github.com/khan-lab/cbio7501-f26>.
2. Click **Code** → **Codespaces** → **Create codespace on main**.
3. Wait a few minutes the first time. You get VS Code in the browser with a
   terminal at the bottom.

::: {.callout-warning title="Codespaces is free only up to a monthly quota"}
On 2026-10-24 GitHub's billing page listed, for free personal accounts, **120
core-hours of compute and 15 GB-month of storage per month** (GitHub Pro: 180
core-hours, 20 GB-month). Our codespace uses a 2-core machine, so that is
about **60 hours a month**. Stop your codespace when you are done (it stops by
itself after 30 minutes idle), and delete old ones at
<https://github.com/codespaces>. Without a payment method on file, GitHub
blocks use once the quota is used up; it resets each month.
:::

## 8. Fill the cache before class

Classroom Wi-Fi gets slow when 30 laptops download the same 2 GB at once. Run
this at home: it downloads the main tools of the course into Pixi's cache (it
runs `samtools` once to show it worked).

```{.bash .run}
pixi exec -c conda-forge -c bioconda \
  --spec fastqc --spec multiqc --spec bwa --spec samtools --spec bcftools \
  -- samtools --version
```

Expected output starts with:

```text
samtools 1.24
Using htslib 1.24
```

On native Windows (not WSL2) this command fails: there are no Windows builds of
these tools. That is expected; use WSL2.

## 9. Setup check

Run the check and keep the output; your instructor may ask for it.

```{.bash .run}
echo "== setup check $(date +%F)"
uname -sm
pixi --version
pixi exec python --version
pixi exec --spec "quarto>=1.9" quarto --version
git --version
```

### Try it yourself

1. Run `pixi exec cowpy "Hello from Pixi"`. Which package did Pixi download,
   and did it install anything on your system?

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   Pixi guessed the package `cowpy` from the command name, downloaded it (and
   Python) into a temporary environment in its cache, and ran it. Nothing was
   added to your `PATH`; the next time you type `cowpy` without `pixi exec`,
   it is not found.
   :::

2. Run `pixi info`. Where is Pixi's cache on your computer, and how big might
   it get?

   ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
   The line `Cache dir` shows it (on macOS `~/Library/Caches/rattler/cache`,
   on Linux `~/.cache/rattler/cache`). It grows with every package version
   you use, easily to several GB. `pixi clean cache` empties it (see
   [Take-down](B-take-down.qmd)).
   :::

## Break it: what "command not found" means

Your shell finds programs by looking in the folders listed in `PATH`. Run
`pixi` with a `PATH` that does not contain Pixi's folder:

```{.bash .expect-fail}
env PATH=/usr/bin:/bin pixi --version
```

```text
env: pixi: No such file or directory
```

Nothing is broken: Pixi is still installed, the shell just does not look in
`~/.pixi/bin`. This is why the installer asks you to open a new terminal, and
why `pixi run` matters later: it puts the project's tools on `PATH` for one
command only.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---------|------------|
| `pixi: command not found` right after installing | Open a new terminal. If it persists, add `export PATH="$HOME/.pixi/bin:$PATH"` to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`. |
| `curl: (6) Could not resolve host` in WSL2 | WSL2 lost its DNS settings. Restart WSL with `wsl --shutdown` in PowerShell and open Ubuntu again. If it persists, ask in class. |
| Downloads time out or are very slow | Try again later or from another network; for a whole class, use the prefetch in step 8 at home. University proxies may need `https_proxy` set. |
| First run of anything on macOS is slow | macOS scans new programs once. Optional: System Settings → Privacy & Security → Developer Tools, add your terminal app. |
| `No space left on device` | Free space or empty Pixi's cache with `pixi clean cache`. |
| `samtools` fails on Windows | Expected: no Windows builds. Use WSL2 or Codespaces. |
| Codespace does not start: quota used | Wait for the monthly reset, use WSL2, or ask the instructor for the lab machines. |

## Key points

- Install Pixi once; projects install everything else through it.
- `pixi exec` runs a tool from a temporary environment without installing it.
- Windows users work in WSL2 (Linux), because key tools have no Windows builds.
- Codespaces is the fallback, within a monthly free quota.
- "Command not found" means "not on `PATH`", not "broken".
